### Auto-regressive hidden Markov model

Let $x_{t}$ denote the six-dimensional vector of nose-head-body coordinates at video frame t (sampled at 80 Hz), with components $(x_{nose},y_{nose},x_{head},y_{head},x_{body},y_{body})$. We fit an AR-HMM to mouse trajectory data, ${x_{t}^{i}}$, across trials (indexed by i) from 13 out of 15 mice (two mice were excluded a priori due to low task performance). These mice performed olfactory search under the following experimental conditions: Variable ΔC, Constant |C| (nine mice); naris occlusion (seven mice); and Constant ΔC, Variable |C| experiments (five mice).

#### The generative view

Viewed as a generative model (that generates simulated data), the AR-HMM has two 'layers': a layer of hidden discrete states (corresponding to discrete movement motifs) and an observed layer that is the continuous trajectory $x_{t}$. We denote the temporal sequence of discrete states by $z_{t}$. In each time step, $z_{t}\in{1,2,…,S}$, that is, it is one of an S number of states, or movement motifs. The discrete hidden states evolve in time according to a Markov chain: going from time step t to t + 1, the discrete state may change to another state according to a transition probability matrix $\pi_{z_{1},z_{2}}$, which denotes the conditional probability of switching to $z_{2}$ having started in $z_{1}$. The probability distribution over the initial state, $z_{t=1}$, of the Markov chain at the start of each trial was taken to be the uniform distribution.

Now suppose for time steps $t_{1}$ to $t_{2}$ (inclusive) the discrete layer remained in state z. The continuous or auto-regressive (AR) part of the model dictates that, over this time interval, the continuous trajectory, $x_{t}$, evolves according to a linear AR process. The parameters of this AR process can be different in different states or motifs, z. In other words, $x_{t}$ is governed by

$$
x_{t}=A_{z}x_{t−1}+b_{z}+\epsilon_{t}.t_{1}\leqt\leqt_{2}
$$

where $A_{z}$ is a 6 × 6 matrix and b is a 6 × 1 vector, and the noise vector $\epsilon_{t}$ is sampled from the multi-variate zero-mean Gaussian distribution $N0,Q_{z}$, where $Q_{z}$ is a 6 × 6 noise covariance matrix. Moreover, the parameters $A_{z}$, $b_{z}$, and $Q_{z}$ depend on the discrete state z, and in general are different in different discrete states. The simple stochastic linear dynamics described by Equation (1) can describe simple motions of the mouse, such as turning left/right, dashing towards a certain direction, freezing (when $A_{z}$ is the identity matrix and $b_{z}$ is zero), etc. The switches between these simple behaviors allow the model to generate complex trajectories.

The AR-HMM is an example of a model with latent variables, which in this case are the discrete state sequence $z_{t}^{i}$ in each trial. The model, as a whole, is specified by the set of parameters ($\pi,{A_{z}},{b_{z}},{Q_{z}}$), which we will denote by $\theta$. For a d-dimensional trajectory (d = 6 here) and S states, comprises $SS-1+Sd^{2}+d+dd+1/2=SS-1+3dd+1/2$ parameters.

#### Model fits

Models with latent variables are often fit using the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm, which maximizes the likelihood of the model in terms of the parameters $\theta≡\pi,{A_{z}},{b_{z}},{Q_{z}}$ for a given set of observed data ${x_{t}^{i}}$. In this work, we did not use the EM algorithm, but adopted a fully Bayesian approach in which both the hidden variables and the model parameters were inferred by drawing samples from their posterior distribution (Wiltschko et al., 2015). The posterior distribution combines the model likelihood and Bayesian priors imposed on its parameters, according to Bayes' rule. If we denote the joint likelihood of observed trajectories, ${x_{t}^{i}}$, and the latent variables, ${z_{t}^{i}}$, by $P{x_{t}^{i},z_{t}^{i}}\theta$ and the prior distribution over model parameters by $P\theta$, then up to normalization, the joint posterior distribution of latent variables and model parameters is given by

$$
P{z_{t}^{i}},\theta{x_{t}^{i}}∝P{x_{t}^{i},z_{t}^{i}}\thetaP\theta.
$$

For the AR-HMM, the (logarithm of the) joint log-likelihood is given by

$$
log⁡P{x_{t}^{i},z_{t}^{i}}\theta=\sum_{i}\sum_{t=2}^{T_{i}}[log⁡\pi_{z_{t-1}^{i},z_{t}^{i}}+logNx_{t}^{i}A_{z_{t}^{i}}x_{t-1}^{i}+b_{z_{t}^{i}},Q_{z_{t}^{i}}].
$$

where $T_{i}$ is the length of trial i, and we use the notation $Nx\mu,Q=e^{-\frac{1}{2}x-\mu^{T}Q^{-1}x-\mu}/\sqrt{2\piQ}$ to denote the density at point x of a multivariate Gaussian with mean vector μ and covariance matrix Q.

We imposed loose conjugate priors on the model parameters, which were factorized over the parameters of the AR process, ${A_{z}},{b_{z}},{Q_{z}}$, in different discrete states z, and the different rows of the Markov transition matrix, $\pi$. On the rows of $\pi$, we imposed Dirichlet distribution priors with uniform distribution means and concentration hyperparameter $\alpha$, which was set to 4. We imposed matrix normal inverse Wishart priors on the AR parameters, independently for different discrete states. Under this prior, the noise covariance $Q_{z}$ has an inverse Wishart distribution with a 'scale matrix' hyperparameter, which was set to the d × d ( = 6 × 6) identity matrix, and a 'degrees-of-freedom' scalar hyperparameter set to d + 2 = 8. Conditional on $Q_{z}$, the remaining AR parameters, $A_{z},b_{z}$, have a joint multivariate normal distribution under the prior, which can be specified by the prior mean and joint prior covariance matrix of $A_{z}$ and $b_{z}$. The prior means of $A_{z}$ and $b_{z}$ were set to the d × d identity matrix and the d-dimensional zero vector, respectively, while the prior covariance matrix of the concatenation $A_{z},b_{z}$ was given by the tensor product of $Q_{z}$ and the (d + 1) × (d + 1)( = 7 × 7) identity matrix (equivalently, under this prior, $b_{z}$ and different columns of $A_{z}$ are independent and uncorrelated, while each of these column vectors has a prior covariance equal to the [prior] AR noise covariance, $Q_{z}$).

Bayesian model inference was carried out by sampling from (instead of maximizing) the joint posterior distribution of the model parameters and latent state variables conditioned on the observed trajectory data (Equation 2). We did this by Gibbs sampling (an example of Markov chain Monte Carlo; not to be confused with the Markov chain in the AR-HMM), which works in a manner conceptually similar to the EM algorithm: it switches between sampling $z_{t}^{i}$ in all trials, conditioned on previously sampled parameters, and then sampling the parameters $\theta$ given the previous sample of ${z_{t}^{i}}$. To carry out this model inference procedure, we used the Python package developed by M.J. Johnson and colleagues, publicly available at https://github.com/mattjj/pyhsmm (Johnson et al., 2013a).

We ran the Gibbs sampler for 300 iterations and burned the first 200 samples, retaining 100. We used the remaining samples to obtain the posterior probabilities of hidden discrete states at each time step of each trial (by calculating the frequency of different state in that time step and trial, across the retained Gibbs samples), as well as posterior expectation of the model parameters (by calculating their averages over the retained Gibbs samples). We refer to the AR-HMM with parameters given by these latter posterior expectations as the ‘fit model’.

#### Model selection

We fit AR-HMM's with different numbers of states (motifs), S, to mouse trajectory data pooled across animals. To evaluate the statistical goodness of fit of these fit model and select the best S (the number of states or motifs), we evaluated the log-likelihoods of fit models on trajectory data from a held-out set of trials, not used for model fitting. The corresponding plot of log-likelihoods is shown in Figure 6F. As seen, the log-likelihood keeps increasing with S, up to S = 100. This shows that, up to at least S = 100, additional motifs do have utility in capturing more variability in mouse trajectories. These variabilities may include differences in movement across mice, as well as movement variations in the same mouse but across different trials or different instances of the same movement; for example, a clockwise head turn executed with different speeds in different instances or trials. In the AR-HMM, the AR observation distribution of a given Markov state corresponds to a very simple (linear) dynamical system that cannot capture many natural and continuous variations in movement, such as changes in movement speed. Nevertheless, AR-HMM models with higher S can capture such variations with more precision by specializing different discrete Markov states, with different AR distributions, to movement motifs of different mice, or, for example, to capture different speeds of the same qualitative movement motif.

The goal for this modeling was to give a compact description of recurring movement features across animals and conditions, suitable for visualization and alignment. For these purposes, the goodness of fit did not provide a suitable criterion because the log-likelihood plots did not peak or plateau even at very large numbers of states. Guided by visual inspection, we thus chose the model with S = 16 for the main figures (Figures 6–8). Although this was a somewhat arbitrary choice, we show that the findings in Figures 6–8 do not depend on the choice of S – models with S = 6, 10, or 20 gave equivalent results (Figure 6—figure supplements 2–4).

#### MAP sequences

The Gibbs sampling algorithm that we used for model inference yields (time-wise marginal) maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimates of the latent variables ${z_{t}^{i}}$, as follows. Using the Gibbs samples for the latent variables, we can estimate the posterior probability of the mouse being in any of the S states in any given time step of a given trial. We made MAP sequences by picking, at any time step and trial, the state with the highest posterior probability. The inferred MAP motifs tended to have high posterior probability, which exceeded 0.8 in 66.2% of all time steps across the 17,195 trials in the modeled dataset.

### Decoding analysis

We decoded experimental conditions and animal identities from single-trial MAP motif sequences inferred using the AR-HMM. Specifically, we trained multi-class decoders with linear decision boundaries (linear discriminant analysis) to decode the above categorical variables from the single-trial empirical state transition probability matrices derived from the MAP sequence of each trial. If $z_{t}^{(i)}^$ is the motif MAP sequence for trial i, the empirical transition probability, $\pi_{a,b}^{(i)}^$, from state a to state $ba,b\in{1,…,K}$, for that trial was calculated by

$$
\pi_{a,b}^{(i)}^≡\frac{n_{a,b}^{(i)}}{\sumc=1Kn_{a,c}^{(i)}}.
$$



$$
n_{a,b}^{(i)}≡\sumt=1T^{(i)}−1I(z_{t}^=a)I(z_{t+1}^=b).
$$

where $T^{i}$ is the length of trial i, and $I⋅$ is an indicator function, returning 1 or 0 when its argument is true or false, respectively.

We used the decoder to either classify experimental condition or mouse identity, in different trials (Figure 6D, E). For decoders trained to classify the trials' experimental condition, we used pooled data across mice. For decoders trained to classify mouse identity, we only used data from the 80:20 odor condition. Data was split into training and test dataset in a stratified fivefold cross-validation manner, ensuring equal proportions of trials of different types in both datasets. The trial type was the combination of left vs. right decision, experimental condition, and mouse identity.

To calculate the statistical significance of decoding accuracies, we performed an iterative shuffle procedure on each fold of the cross-validation. In each shuffle, the training labels that the classifier was trained to decode were shuffled randomly across trials of the training set, and the classifier's accuracy was evaluated on the unshuffled test dataset. This shuffle was performed 100 times to create a shuffle distribution of decoding accuracies for each fold of the cross-validation. From these distributions, we calculated the z-score of decoding accuracy for each class in each cross-validation fold. These z-scores were then averaged across the folds of cross-validation and used to calculate the overall p-value of the decoding accuracy obtained on the original data.

Reviewer #2:

In this study, Smear et al. aim to investigate how mice sample the noisy stimulus information from olfactory plumes such as to navigate towards their source. To this end, they developed a 2AFC task for freely moving mice where the same odor emanates from two lateral sources, at independently controllable concentrations. Mice are required to identify the more intense of the two sources and collect water from reward port located on the side with the higher odor concentration. The authors improve on previous attempts at studying this problem by requiring the mice to commit to their decision at a substantial distance from the odor ports. This forces the mice to assess odor concentration from distal cues rather than via serial sampling of the sources themselves. Interestingly, the authors find that stereo olfaction (comparing concentration across two nostrils) is not required to determine source location from distal cues. Using a series of stimulus conditions, the authors convincingly show that in their paradigm, mice rely on olfactory cues and specifically the relative, not absolute, concentration difference between the two sources.

The relevance of stereo olfaction for airborne odor cues has been long debated. In my opinion, the authors results in principle resolve this debate – stereo comparisons allow finer source localisation near the source, while serial sampling may play a larger role farther away from source. One concern however is that this lack of reliance on stereo sampling may result from the specific task design and the constraints it imposes on the behavior (see concerns).

Further, the authors characterise the sampling behaviors of mice during this task by monitoring respiration (thermistor) as well as nose, head and body positions (video tracking). The authors find a striking, active synchronisation of sniffing and nose (and body) movements that gets selectively recruited during putative investigatory phase of the task i.e. when mice are actively exploring the concentration gradient. The authors do exhaustive analysis to show that such synchronisation is not a default state and the coupling is much weaker during other phases within the same trial. While such coupling of movement and intrinsic rhythms has been proposed previously, to my knowledge this is the first careful characterisation of this phenomenon in freely moving mice. Importantly, the authors results not only confirm the existence of such coupling but also clarify that this synchronisation is an active feature of olfactory navigation. Interestingly however, the authors do not find any significant difference in sampling strategies across different stimulus difficulties (see concerns).

Lastly, the authors use machine learning to parse motion trajectories into identifiable behavioral motifs. With their approach, they find that a range of motifs that are stereotyped across mice and occur in non-random sequences during each trial. Further, a trained decoder can successfully decode mouse identity from the sequences in which these motifs in each animal. While these motif based analysis are well done, the data presented do not seem to make any clear predictions about how these motif sequences would change in different task conditions. The authors do not find any obvious relationship between trial types (difficult versus easy stimuli) and motif sequences and the presented analyses do not add much to the main message of the paper. I therefore lack the imagination to accurately assess the relevance of this portion of the study.

Overall, the study is well executed – the data presented are clear with numerous controls at each step. In my opinion, the evidence provided for lack of need for stereo olfaction for distal source assessment and active synchronisation of sniffing and sampling movements are important contributions to the field of olfaction that warrant publication in eLife. However, I have several conceptual concern about the task design and the interpretations of the results that the authors should clarify prior to publication.

1. My primary concern is about the task design. I commend the authors for the careful control of olfactory stimuli and substantial improvements over previously published odor localisation assays by separating the reward port from the odor source and forcing decisions at locations distant from the source. However, the task design chosen does not really require the mice to localize odor sources beyond just indicating whether there is more odor on the right versus left. This is different from natural conditions, where the necessary spatial resolution may be much higher. In fact, finer source localization confers no additional benefit for maximizing reward in this task. Therefore, the sampling strategies exhibited by the subjects here may be different from those employed during natural odor navigation where the motivation is to precisely locate the source of mate, food or predators.

2. Along the same lines, it is surprising that even for the easiest version of the task, the performance hovers around 80%, even though PID characterisations show very clear differences between the two halves of the arena. Furthermore, performance drops with increasing stimulus difficulty but mice do not appear to change their sampling strategies to compensate for the lower reward rate. I am trying to reconcile these two facts. At first pass, given known olfactory acuity of rodents, it seems that trained mice should have no trouble handling the easiest stimuli (reach almost 100% success). One possibility is that the mice are not fully motivated/engaged in the task. An alternate explanation is that mice are fully motivated to reach maximum reward rate, but the task is just too hard and the sampling strategies employed at 100:0 condition are their best, and therefore with increasing stimulus difficulty, they cannot perform any better. Yet, the latter possibility appears very unlikely. Can the authors comment on these two possibilities? The question remains whether mice when pushed to achieve higher performances would employ different sampling strategies.

3. Lastly, looking at Figure 5Ai it appears that overall nose speeds are significantly lower during ITI than during the investigatory bouts within the trial. While the authors rule out that sniffing-movement synchronisation is simply a feature of rapid sniffing, they do not rule out the dependence on running speeds. Perhaps the apparent lack of synchrony in ITI results from poorer ability to resolve decelerations, given lower speeds on average. This is also consistent with reduced, but significant synchrony during premature initiations in the ITI (Figure S7A) where speeds tend to be higher than those shown in Figure 5Ai. This should be easily addressable by repeating the analysis on speed matched datasets.

Together with panel 3D, it suggests that mice undergo fairly stereotyped searches: after poking their nose out of the initiation port, they appear to make a 180 degree rotation (sweep) to face the gradient. The density reaches a maximum at that point (opposite to the position of the initiation port). Is this position (crossing of the alpha shape) dominated by an "investigation" state? Can this position be viewed as a decision point? When/where does the animal tend switch to the "approach" state? More generally, could you map dominate trends in behavioral motifs of Figure 6B onto the stereotyped alpha shape of the occupancy diagram of Figure 3F?

3. Figure 2D: Could you speculate about the reason why trials tend to be longer for the 100:0 conditions compared to the more difficult 60:40? Do mice spend more time in the investigation phase when gradient is stronger? Although this result would be counter-intuitive, it might suggest that mice learn (?) to spend less time on the initial search when less information is available to them.

4. Figure 1D indicates that the average gradient's geometry is not the same when the odor is delivered on the left side (100:0) compared to the right side (0:100). This observation appears to be true for the other odor ratios reported in Figure S2. This asymmetry should affect the gradient that the animal experiences during the investigation phase, which should in turn influence the accuracy of the decisions. Do you expect a 50:50 condition to produce no preference (on average)?

5. Figure 7F: What are you concluding from this panel? Are you sure that the shaded areas represent the standard deviation and not the SEM? If the standard deviation is shown, how do you explain the existence of stereotypical wiggles on a timescale of 50 ms? It would be very useful to represent a variant of Figure 7C where the trials are sorted between correct and incorrect.

claims.claim: Mice solve the olfactory search task using concentration gradient cues.
claims.source: Mice solve this task using concentration gradient cues and do not require stereo olfaction for performance.
claims.evidence: The manuscript presents behavioral experiments showing that performance varies with concentration gradients (Figure 2D) and that mice perform equally well with different absolute concentrations when the gradient is held constant (Figure 2E).

claims.claim: Mice do not require stereo olfaction for performance in the olfactory search task.
claims.source: Mice solve this task using concentration gradient cues and do not require stereo olfaction for performance.
claims.evidence: Naris occlusion experiments (Figure 2F) showed no significant impact on performance, indicating stereo olfaction is not necessary.

claims.claim: Respiration and nose movement are synchronized with tens of milliseconds precision during task performance.
claims.source: During task performance, respiration and nose movement are synchronized with tens of milliseconds precision.
claims.evidence: Figure 5 shows sniff-aligned kinematic parameters demonstrating precise temporal synchronization between nose movements and sniffing.

claims.claim: Sniff-synchronized nose movement is present during trials and largely absent during inter-trial intervals.
claims.source: This synchrony is present during trials and largely absent during inter-trial intervals, suggesting that sniff-synchronized nose movement is a strategic behavioral state rather than simply a constant accompaniment to fast breathing.
claims.evidence: Figure 5 demonstrates reduced kinematic synchrony during ITI compared to within-trial periods, even when controlling for nose speed.

claims.claim: Sniff-synchronized nose movement is a strategic behavioral state rather than a constant accompaniment to fast breathing.
claims.source: This synchrony is present during trials and largely absent during inter-trial intervals, suggesting that sniff-synchronized nose movement is a strategic behavioral state rather than simply a constant accompaniment to fast breathing.
claims.evidence: The differential presence of synchrony during task performance versus ITI, and its presence during premature initiation attempts, suggests strategic deployment.

claims.claim: Movement motifs fall into two clusters corresponding to investigation and approach states.
claims.source: Motifs fall into two clusters, which correspond to investigation and approach states.
claims.evidence: Figure 7A shows clustering of the transition probability matrix revealing two distinct blocks of motifs labeled as investigation and approach.

claims.claim: Investigation motifs lock precisely to sniffing at specific phases of the sniff cycle.
claims.source: Investigation motifs lock precisely to sniffing, such that the individual motifs preferentially occur at specific phases of the sniff cycle.
claims.evidence: Figure 8 shows that investigation motifs have significantly higher modulation indices in both time and phase coordinates relative to sniff cycles.

claims.claim: The allocentric structure of investigation and approach indicates an advantage to sampling both sides of the sharpest part of the odor gradient.
claims.source: The allocentric structure of investigation and approach indicates an advantage to sampling both sides of the sharpest part of the odor gradient, consistent with a serial-sniff strategy for gradient sensing.
claims.evidence: Figure 10 shows that correct trials feature significantly increased investigation at and on the unchosen side of the midline, where gradients are steepest.

claims.claim: The allocentric structure of investigation and approach is consistent with a serial-sniff strategy for gradient sensing.
claims.source: The allocentric structure of investigation and approach indicates an advantage to sampling both sides of the sharpest part of the odor gradient, consistent with a serial-sniff strategy for gradient sensing.
claims.evidence: The spatial pattern of investigation occupancy across the midline supports serial comparison of odor concentrations across sniffs rather than single-sniff absolute concentration judgments.

claims.claim: Almost all mice performed above chance in the first session of the 100:0 odor search task.
claims.source: Almost all mice performed above chance in the first session (Figure 2B; binomial test, p<0.05 for 24 out of 25 mice, 75 ± 9.2% correct, mean ± sd).
claims.evidence: Statistical testing with binomial test showed 24 out of 25 mice performed significantly above chance.

claims.claim: Within four sessions of 100:0 training, most animals exceeded 80% performance.
claims.source: Within four sessions, most animals exceeded 80% performance (19 out of 26).
claims.evidence: Behavioral training data showing progression of performance across sessions.

claims.claim: Mice generalize olfactory search behavior to novel odorants.
claims.source: We found no differences in performance between vanillin and pinene sessions for these mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A; Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=0.827, n = 3).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison showed no significant difference in performance when switching from pinene to vanillin.

claims.claim: Olfactory search behavior does not rely on the trigeminal system.
claims.source: We found no differences in performance between vanillin and pinene sessions for these mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A; Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=0.827, n = 3). These data suggest that this search behavior generalizes across odors and does not rely on the trigeminal system.
claims.evidence: Vanillin does not activate trigeminal fibers (Cometto-Muñiz and Abraham, 2010; Doty et al., 1978; Hummel et al., 2009), yet performance was equivalent to pinene.

claims.claim: On odor omission probe trials, mice performed at chance level.
claims.source: On these probe trials, mice performed at chance (binomial test, p=0.9989), with longer trial durations (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05) and more tortuous trajectories (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05) than on non-probe trials (Figure 2C; n = 19, all data from 80:20 condition with probe trials).
claims.evidence: Statistical testing showed performance was not significantly different from chance on 0:0 trials.

claims.claim: Performance drops with decreasing concentration ratio.
claims.source: Performance drops with the concentration ratio (ΔC), consistent with our reasoning that mice would use odor gradient cues in this task (Figure 2D; pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, p<0.05, n = 15).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison across concentration ratios (100:0, 80:20, 60:40) showed significant differences in performance.

claims.claim: Odor gradients guide olfactory search under turbulent conditions.
claims.source: These results indicate that odor gradients guide olfactory search under these conditions.
claims.evidence: Equal performance in 90:30 and 30:10 conditions demonstrates gradient-based rather than absolute concentration-based navigation.

claims.claim: Naris occlusion does not significantly impact performance or path tortuosity in the olfactory search task.
claims.source: We found that naris occlusion did not significantly impact performance or path tortuosity (pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, p>0.05).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison between naris occlusion, sham, and no-stitch conditions showed no significant differences in performance or tortuosity.

claims.claim: Stereo comparison is not necessary for the olfactory search task.
claims.source: These overall results indicate that stereo comparison is not necessary in this task (Figure 2F; n = 13), and that temporal comparisons across sniffs (Catania, 2013; Parabucki et al., 2019) play a larger role under our task conditions.
claims.evidence: Naris occlusion experiments showed no significant performance deficits, indicating stereo cues are not required.

claims.claim: Temporal comparisons across sniffs play a larger role than stereo comparisons in the olfactory search task.
claims.source: These overall results indicate that stereo comparison is not necessary in this task (Figure 2F; n = 13), and that temporal comparisons across sniffs (Catania, 2013; Parabucki et al., 2019) play a larger role under our task conditions.
claims.evidence: The lack of stereo requirement combined with gradient-based navigation suggests serial-sniff comparisons are the primary strategy.

claims.claim: Inhalation and sniff durations are shorter during trials than during inter-trial intervals.
claims.source: In this active behavioral state, inhalation and sniff durations were shorter during trials than during ITIs (p<<0.01 for all mice; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test; Figure 3B, C)
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of sniff parameters between trial and ITI periods showed significant differences.

claims.claim: Sniff durations during the task are strikingly shorter than those observed in head-fixed rodents.
claims.source: In this active behavioral state, inhalation and sniff durations were shorter during trials than during ITIs (p<<0.01 for all mice; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test; Figure 3B, C), and strikingly shorter than those observed in head-fixed rodents (Bolding and Franks, 2017; Shusterman et al., 2011; Wesson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Comparison with published data from head-fixed preparations shows qualitatively faster sniffing in freely moving mice.

claims.claim: Nose speed accelerates during exhalation, peaks at inhalation onset, and decelerates during inhalation.
claims.source: On average, nose speed accelerates during exhalation, peaks at inhalation onset, and decelerates during inhalation (Figure 5Ai).
claims.evidence: Sniff-aligned kinematic analysis shows consistent temporal relationship between nose speed and sniff phase.

claims.claim: Head yaw velocity reaches peak centrifugal velocity at inhalation and moves centripetally over the course of inhalation.
claims.source: Head yaw velocity, which we define as toward or away (Figure 4; centripetal or centrifugal) from the body-head axis, reaches peak centrifugal velocity at inhalation, decelerates and moves centripetally over the course of inhalation (Figure 5Aii).
claims.evidence: Sniff-aligned analysis of yaw velocity shows consistent phase relationship with sniff cycle.

claims.claim: Z-velocity reaches peak upward velocity at inhalation onset, decelerates and goes downward during inhalation, and rises again at exhalation.
claims.source: The Z-velocity reaches peak upward velocity at inhalation onset, decelerates and goes downward during inhalation, and rises again at exhalation (Figure 5Aiii).
claims.evidence: Sniff-aligned analysis of Z-velocity (distance between snout and head) shows consistent phase relationship with sniff cycle.

claims.claim: Kinematic modulations during trials are absent from trial-shuffled data.
claims.source: These modulations were absent from trial-shuffled data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; permutation test, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: Permutation testing demonstrates that observed kinematic synchrony exceeds what would be expected by chance.

claims.claim: Sniff synchrony is significantly reduced during the inter-trial interval compared to within-trial periods.
claims.source: For nose speed, yaw velocity, and Z-velocity, sniff synchrony is significantly reduced during the ITI when the mouse is returning from the reward port to initiate the next trial, even when the mouse is sniffing rapidly.
claims.evidence: Figure 5 shows reduced modulation of kinematic parameters during ITI compared to trial periods.

claims.claim: The difference in kinematic synchrony between within-trial and inter-trial intervals is not contingent on nose speed.
claims.source: This difference between within-trial and between-trial sniff synchrony was not contingent on the mouse's slower nose speed during the ITI (Figure 5A). Kinematic synchrony was the same when only periods of high-speed nose movement in the ITI are included in the analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Analysis controlling for nose speed shows that synchrony differences persist, indicating they are not simply due to movement speed.

claims.claim: Sniff-synchronized movement is a proactive, odor-seeking strategy rather than a reactive, odor-gated reflex.
claims.source: Taken together, our observations indicate that sniff synchronous movement is a proactive, odor-seeking strategy rather than a reactive, odor-gated reflex.
claims.evidence: The selective deployment of synchrony during task performance, its presence during premature initiations, and its reduction post-decision all support a strategic rather than reflexive interpretation.

claims.claim: The AR-HMM model identifies discrete movement patterns (motifs) that recur throughout the dataset.
claims.source: These models defined discrete movement patterns, or 'motifs', that recur throughout our dataset (e.g., Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The AR-HMM successfully parsed continuous movement data into recurring discrete motifs as shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Mice can be identified from motif sequences on a trial-by-trial basis above chance for eight out of nine mice.
claims.source: A classifier trained to decode mouse identity from the motif sequences on a trial-by-trial basis was able to perform above chance for eight out of nine mice (Figure 6D; p<0.01).
claims.evidence: Linear decoder analysis with permutation testing showed significant above-chance decoding of mouse identity.

claims.claim: Movement sequences are not statistically distinguishable across different concentration ratios.
claims.source: Across the different concentration ratios (Figure 2D), movement sequences were not statistically distinguishable (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Linear decoder analysis failed to distinguish between concentration ratio conditions based on motif sequences.

claims.claim: Odor omission trials give distinguishable motif patterns compared to odorized trials.
claims.source: The only condition that gave distinguishable motif patterns were the odor omission trials (0:0), in which the mice made longer, more tortuous trajectories (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Linear decoder successfully distinguished 0:0 trials from odorized trials based on motif sequences.

claims.claim: Mice do not modify their sampling behavior in a gradient-dependent manner.
claims.source: Thus, although this model is sensitive enough to decode mouse identity (Figure 6D), it does not detect stimulus-dependent modifications of sampling behavior, suggesting that the mice do not modify their sampling behavior in a gradient-dependent manner, at least in the movement parameters we measured.
claims.evidence: The inability to decode concentration ratios from motif sequences suggests lack of adaptive strategy across gradient conditions.

claims.claim: Clustering of motifs by transition probabilities separates them into two groups corresponding to investigation and approach.
claims.source: To reveal higher-order structure in the temporal organization of these motifs, we applied a clustering algorithm that minimizes the Euclidean distance between rows of the Markov transition matrix (i.e., purely based on the conditional probabilities of motifs following them). This clustering separated motifs into two groups (Figure 7A), with several distinct properties.
claims.evidence: Hierarchical clustering of the transition probability matrix revealed two distinct blocks of motifs.

claims.claim: Investigation motifs tend to occur early in trials while approach motifs tend to occur later.
claims.source: First, investigation and approach motifs cluster their onset times in the trial, with investigation motifs tending to occur early in the trial, while approach motifs tend to begin later (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: Analysis of motif onset times shows temporal segregation between investigation and approach states.

claims.claim: Trials begin with investigation and end with approach.
claims.source: Grouping motifs into these higher-order states shows a consistent trial sequence, with trials beginning with investigation and ending with approach (Figure 7C, D).
claims.evidence: Visualization of state sequences across trials shows consistent temporal progression from investigation to approach.

claims.claim: Switches from approach back to investigation are common during trials.
claims.source: Importantly, entering the approach state is not a final, ballistic commitment to a given water port – switches from approach back to investigation were common (Figure 7C, D, Video 7).
claims.evidence: State sequence analysis shows frequent transitions from approach back to investigation within trials.

claims.claim: Mice continuously integrate evidence about the odor gradient throughout their trajectory to the target.
claims.source: This pattern suggests that the mice are continuously integrating evidence about the odor gradient throughout their trajectory to the target.
claims.evidence: The frequent switches between approach and investigation states indicate ongoing sensory evaluation rather than ballistic commitment.

claims.claim: During investigation motifs, mice move more slowly and sniff more rapidly than during approach motifs.
claims.source: During investigation motifs, the mice moved more slowly and sniffed more rapidly, whereas the approach states were associated with faster movement and slower sniffing (Figure 7E)
claims.evidence: Quantitative comparison of nose speed and sniff rate between investigation and approach states shows significant differences.

claims.claim: Sniff-synchronized kinematic rhythms are distinct between investigation and approach states.
claims.source: Third, the sniff-synchronized kinematic rhythms (Figures 4 and 5) were distinct in the two states (Figure 7F; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p<0.01).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of sniff-aligned kinematic parameters shows significant differences between states.

claims.claim: Nose speed and yaw velocity are more synchronized with sniffing during the investigation state than the approach state.
claims.source: Specifically, nose speed and yaw velocity are more synchronized with sniffing during the investigation state (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Modulation index analysis shows higher synchrony for nose speed and yaw velocity during investigation compared to approach.

claims.claim: Nose speed and yaw velocity modulation between investigation and approach states exceeds what would be expected from across-trial tendencies.
claims.source: This analysis showed that nose speed and yaw velocity modulation exceeded what would be expected from across-trial tendencies (1000 shuffles, p<0.001), while the Z-velocity modulation did not (p=0.31).
claims.evidence: Permutation testing demonstrates that kinematic differences between states are not artifacts of temporal structure.

claims.claim: All investigation motifs are significantly modulated in both time and phase coordinates relative to sniffing.
claims.source: All investigation motifs were significantly modulated for both time and phase coordinates (Figure 8E; filled symbols, permutation test, p<0.001), with some having higher MI in time, and others in phase.
claims.evidence: Statistical testing of modulation indices shows significant sniff-locking for all investigation motifs.

claims.claim: Investigation motifs lock to the sniff cycle with precision at a tens of milliseconds scale.
claims.source: Temporally, investigation motifs lock to the sniff cycle with precision at a tens of milliseconds scale.
claims.evidence: Analysis of motif onset times relative to sniff phase shows precise temporal locking (Figure 8).

claims.claim: Mice primarily investigate near the initiation port and primarily approach close to the decision line.
claims.source: As expected from the temporal structure of investigation and approach (Figure 7C, D), the mice primarily investigate near the initiation port (Figure 9A; n = 9 mice) and primarily approach close to the decision line (Figure 9A, orange).
claims.evidence: Spatial occupancy maps show distinct spatial distributions of investigation and approach states.

claims.claim: The overlap region between investigation and approach occupancy is displaced toward the chosen side of the arena.
claims.source: However, if trials are oriented such that the chosen side is always up in the occupancy maps, the overlap region is displaced toward the chosen side of the arena in all individual mice (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Analysis of occupancy maps aligned to choice shows consistent bias toward the chosen side across mice.

claims.claim: Mice primarily switch from investigation to approach while located on the side they ultimately choose.
claims.source: Thus, the mice primarily switched states while located on the side they would ultimately choose.
claims.evidence: Spatial analysis of state transitions shows they occur preferentially on the chosen side.

claims.claim: Most transitions between investigation and approach occur in a transition zone between 5 and 10 cm from the initiation port.
claims.source: Along the longitudinal axis, most of the change in this index occurred between inflection points at 5 and 10 cm, which we define as a 'transition zone' for the analyses below (Figure 9D).
claims.evidence: Analysis of the investigation-approach index along the longitudinal axis identifies a specific spatial region of state transitions.

claims.claim: Correct trials feature significantly higher investigation in the latter part of the transition zone compared to incorrect trials.
claims.source: Correct trials featured significantly higher I.A.I. (greater investigation) in the latter part of the transition zone, while past the decision zone the I.A.I. was higher for incorrect trials (Figure 10C; permutation test, p<0.001, n = 9 mice).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of investigation-approach index between correct and incorrect trials shows significant spatial differences.

claims.claim: Increased investigation in the transition zone is associated with correct trials.
claims.source: Thus, increased investigation in the transition zone was associated with correct trials, while increased investigation near the decision line was associated with incorrect trials.
claims.evidence: Spatial analysis shows that where investigation occurs matters for task performance.

claims.claim: Investigation is not inherently advantageous to olfactory search irrespective of location.
claims.source: This pattern suggests that investigation is not inherently advantageous to olfactory search irrespective of location. Instead, it matters where the mouse investigates, and some locations are less advantageous.
claims.evidence: The differential association of investigation with correct vs. incorrect trials depending on location indicates spatial specificity of advantage.

claims.claim: Mice may not be able to capitalize on absolute concentration cues near the decision line.
claims.source: Notably, absolute concentrations are most discriminable near the decision line (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that mice may not be able to capitalize on this cue under these conditions.
claims.evidence: The association of increased investigation near the decision line with incorrect trials, despite this being where absolute concentrations are most discriminable, suggests inability to use this cue.

claims.claim: Correct trials feature significantly increased investigation at and on the unchosen side of the midline relative to incorrect trials.
claims.source: Correct trials featured significantly increased investigation at and on the unchosen side of the midline relative to incorrect trials (Figure 10G; permutation test, p<0.001, n = 9 mice).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of investigation occupancy along the lateral axis shows significant differences between correct and incorrect trials.

claims.claim: Sampling both sides of the midline is advantageous for task performance.
claims.source: This suggests an advantage to sampling both sides of the midline, consistent with a serial-sniff gradient sensing strategy.
claims.evidence: The increased investigation on the unchosen side in correct trials indicates benefit from bilateral sampling.

claims.claim: Investigation more laterally, downwind of the odor port, is increased on incorrect trials.
claims.source: Further, investigation more laterally, downwind of the odor port, was increased on incorrect trials, suggesting that sampling this location was not advantageous for task performance, contrary to the single-sniff absolute concentration hypothesis.
claims.evidence: Spatial analysis shows that investigation directly downwind of odor sources is associated with incorrect trials.

claims.claim: Sampling directly downwind of odor sources is not advantageous for task performance.
claims.source: Further, investigation more laterally, downwind of the odor port, was increased on incorrect trials, suggesting that sampling this location was not advantageous for task performance, contrary to the single-sniff absolute concentration hypothesis.
claims.evidence: The association of downwind investigation with incorrect trials contradicts predictions of a single-sniff absolute concentration strategy.

claims.claim: Both stay and switch trials show significantly increased investigation at and on the unchosen side of the midline for correct trials.
claims.source: Although not identical, both stay and switch trials showed significantly increased investigation at and on the unchosen side of the midline for correct trials (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Separate analysis of stay and switch trials shows consistent pattern of midline crossing advantage.

claims.claim: The apparent advantage of sampling across the midline is not an artifact of the asymmetry between switch and stay trials.
claims.source: This analysis demonstrates that the apparent advantage of sampling across the midline is not an artifact of the asymmetry between switch and stay trials.
claims.evidence: Control analysis separating trial types rules out confounding explanation for midline sampling advantage.

claims.claim: Mice use a serial-sniff strategy to sense gradient cues in the olfactory search task.
claims.source: Taken together, investigation and approach occupancy mapping provides further evidence, suggesting that mice use a serial-sniff strategy to sense gradient cues in this task (Catania, 2013).
claims.evidence: The spatial pattern of investigation occupancy, particularly the advantage of sampling across the midline, supports serial comparison of odor concentrations.

claims.claim: Mice can navigate noisy gradients formed by turbulent odor plumes.
claims.source: Taken together, these results show that mice can navigate noisy gradients formed by turbulent odor plumes.
claims.evidence: Successful task performance with varying gradients in turbulent flow conditions demonstrates this capability.

claims.claim: Gradient-guided search is robust to novel odorant introduction.
claims.source: This gradient-guided search is robust to perturbations including novel odorant introduction and naris occlusion.
claims.evidence: Experiments with vanillin and naris occlusion showed maintained performance.

claims.claim: Mice synchronize rapid three-dimensional head movements with fast sniffing during search.
claims.source: During search, mice synchronize rapid three-dimensional head movements with fast sniffing.
claims.evidence: Analysis of nose speed, yaw velocity, and Z-velocity shows precise temporal coordination with sniff cycle.

claims.claim: Movement trajectories vary considerably across trials.
claims.source: Movement trajectories are not stereotyped, but vary considerably across trials.
claims.evidence: Visualization of nose trajectories shows high trial-to-trial variability (Figure 3D).

claims.claim: Individual mice can be identified by how they sequence motifs.
claims.source: This analysis captures common movement features across mice, but individual mice can be identified by how they sequence these motifs.
claims.evidence: Linear decoder successfully identified individual mice from motif sequences above chance.

claims.claim: The onset times of motifs are precisely locked to sniffing.
claims.source: Lastly, the onset times of motifs were precisely locked to sniffing, with investigation motifs starting at characteristic phases of the sniff cycle.
claims.evidence: Analysis of motif onset times relative to sniff phase shows significant temporal locking.

claims.claim: Incorrect trials feature more investigation directly downwind of the odor source.
claims.source: Notably, incorrect trials feature more investigation directly downwind of the odor source, along the axis of maximal odor concentration, which would be optimal if the mouse were using a single-sniff, absolute concentration strategy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: Spatial analysis shows increased investigation in regions of maximal absolute concentration on incorrect trials.

claims.claim: Mice do not capitalize on absolute concentration information to guide performance in the olfactory search task.
claims.source: Thus, these analyses provide further evidence that the mice do not capitalize on absolute concentration information to guide performance in this task.
claims.evidence: The pattern of investigation occupancy contradicts predictions of an absolute concentration strategy.

claims.claim: Correct trials feature more investigation at and across the axis of maximal odor gradient.
claims.source: Instead, correct trials feature more investigation at and across the axis of maximal odor gradient (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), reminiscent of an object localization strategy observed in Egyptian fruit bats.
claims.evidence: Spatial analysis shows increased investigation in regions of maximal gradient on correct trials.

claims.claim: Egyptian fruit bats point their sonar beams off axis so that the maximum slope of the acoustic profile intersects the object when approaching it.
claims.source: When approaching an object, these bats do not center their sonar beams directly at the object, but rather point them off axis, so that the maximum slope of the acoustic profile intersects the object (Yovel et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Citation of published work on bat echolocation strategy.

claims.claim: Mice perform best when they investigate the location of the steepest slope of the odor gradient.
claims.source: Likewise, in this task mice do not gain an advantage by centering their sniffing directly downwind of the odor sources, but rather perform best when they investigate the location of the steepest slope of the odor gradient, consistent with a serial-sniff gradient sensing strategy.
claims.evidence: Spatial analysis of investigation occupancy shows advantage for sampling at the steepest gradient.

claims.claim: Sampling off axis can be an optimal strategy for localization across diverse sensory systems and species.
claims.source: Thus, our unsupervised computational analysis of airborne odor tracking supports the idea that sampling off axis can be an optimal strategy for localization across diverse sensory systems and species (Yovel et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The parallel between mouse olfactory search and bat echolocation suggests a general principle of sensory localization.

claims.claim: Some organisms operate in a regime where diffusion forms smooth chemical gradients suitable for classical chemotaxis strategies.
claims.source: Some organisms operate in a regime where diffusion forms smooth chemical gradients, in which classical chemotaxis strategies can be effective (Bargmann, 2006; Berg, 2000; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012; Lockery, 2011).
claims.evidence: Citation of established literature on chemotaxis in small organisms.

claims.claim: Flying insects often operate in a highly turbulent regime where concentration gradients are not reliably informative.
claims.source: In contrast, other organisms, such as flying insects, often operate in a highly turbulent regime where concentration gradients are not reliably informative (Crimaldi et al., 2002; Murlis et al., 1992; Riffell et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Citation of established literature on insect olfactory navigation in turbulent conditions.

claims.claim: Mice in the olfactory search task operate in an intermediate regime where turbulent odor plumes close to the ground form noisy gradients.
claims.source: By design, mice in our task operate in an intermediate regime, where turbulent odor plumes close to the ground form noisy gradients (Gire et al., 2016; Riffell et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Task design and PID measurements show turbulent flow with noisy but present gradients.

claims.claim: Mice are guided by gradient cues in the intermediate turbulent regime.
claims.source: Because behavior varies with the gradient and not the absolute concentration (Figure 2C–E), we have shown that mice are guided by gradient cues in this regime.
claims.evidence: Behavioral experiments varying gradient and absolute concentration independently demonstrate gradient-based navigation.

claims.claim: Performance is higher when mice sample both sides of the midline.
claims.source: Further, performance is higher when the mice sample both sides of the midline, suggesting that they sense the gradient by comparing sniff sequences across time.
claims.evidence: Spatial analysis of investigation occupancy shows advantage for bilateral sampling.

claims.claim: Stereo manipulations had small but significant effects on performance in odor trail following studies.
claims.source: This finding contrasts with previous studies of olfactory navigation in a different regime: following a depositional odor trail. In these studies, stereo manipulations had small but significant effects on performance, and led to changes in movement strategy (Jones and Urban, 2018; Khan et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Citation of published work on stereo olfaction in trail following.

claims.claim: Stereo reversal in moles did not affect navigation at a distance from the target but reversed turning behavior near the target.
claims.source: Importantly, a study of olfactory search in moles showed that stereo reversal did not affect navigation at a distance from the target, but reversed turning behavior in the target's immediate vicinity (Catania, 2013).
claims.evidence: Citation of published work on stereo olfaction in moles.

claims.claim: Stereo cues may be informative near a source where gradients are steep but play less of a role at greater distance where gradients are more shallow.
claims.source: These results suggest that stereo cues may be informative near a source, where gradients are steep, but that stereo cues play less of a role at a greater distance from the source where gradients are more shallow.
claims.evidence: Synthesis of findings from multiple studies on stereo olfaction.

claims.claim: The task design forces mice out of the stereo regime and into the serial-sniff comparison regime.
claims.source: We propose that our task design, in which mice must commit to a side at a distance from the source, forces mice out of the stereo regime and into the serial-sniff comparison regime.
claims.evidence: Task design with distant decision line combined with naris occlusion results supports this interpretation.

claims.claim: Neurons sensitive to sniff-to-sniff odor concentration changes have been observed in the olfactory bulb of head-fixed mice.
claims.source: Neurons sensitive to sniff-to-sniff odor concentration changes have been observed in the olfactory bulb of head-fixed mice (Parabucki et al., 2019), providing a potential physiological mechanism for this sensory computation.
claims.evidence: Citation of published physiological work on concentration change detection.

claims.claim: The external stimulus obtained by moving the nose through a noisy gradient differs dramatically from square odor pulses delivered during head-fixed tasks.
claims.source: The external stimulus obtained by moving the nose through a noisy gradient differs dramatically from the square odor pulses delivered during head-fixed or odor-poke olfactory tasks.
claims.evidence: Comparison of stimulus conditions between freely moving and head-fixed paradigms.

claims.claim: Sniff statistics in freely moving mice performing olfactory search are qualitatively faster than those reported in head-fixed mice under most conditions.
claims.source: Further, the sniff statistics we observe in our mice are qualitatively faster than those reported in head-fixed mice under most conditions (Bolding and Franks, 2017; Shusterman et al., 2011; Wesson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Comparison of measured sniff durations with published data from head-fixed preparations.

claims.claim: Mice sniff fast in response to a novel odor.
claims.source: One exception is that mice sniff fast in response to a novel odor (Wesson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Citation of published work on novelty-evoked fast sniffing.

claims.claim: Fast stimulation impacts the responsiveness of olfactory sensory neurons.
claims.source: Such fast stimulation impacts the responsiveness of olfactory sensory neurons (Esclassan et al., 2012; Ghatpande and Reisert, 2011; Verhagen et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Citation of published physiological work on effects of fast sniffing on sensory neurons.

claims.claim: Short- and long-term synaptic and network plasticity mechanisms influence the olfactory bulb's responses during fast sniffing.
claims.source: In addition to the temporal properties of odor transduction, short- and long-term synaptic and network plasticity mechanisms will influence the olfactory bulb's responses during fast sniffing (Beshel et al., 2007; Díaz-Quesada et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2015; Jordan et al., 2018; Mandairon and Linster, 2009; Patterson et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Citation of published work on plasticity mechanisms in olfactory bulb.

claims.claim: Understanding gained from head-fixed studies in olfaction will be incomplete without tapping into the fast sniffing regime.
claims.source: Without tapping into the fast sniffing regime, the understanding we can gain from head-fixed studies in olfaction will be incomplete at best.
claims.evidence: Logical argument based on differences between head-fixed and freely moving conditions.

claims.claim: Rodents investigate their environment with active sniffing and whisking behaviors.
claims.source: It has long been known that rodents investigate their environment with active sniffing and whisking behaviors (Kepecs et al., 2006; Wachowiak, 2011; Welker, 1964).
claims.evidence: Citation of established literature on rodent active sensing.

claims.claim: Under some conditions, sniffing locks with whisking, nose twitches, and head movement on a cycle-by-cycle basis.
claims.source: More recent work has established that under some conditions sniffing locks with whisking, nose twitches, and head movement on a cycle-by-cycle basis (Kurnikova et al., 2017; Moore et al., 2013; Ranade et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Citation of published work on sensorimotor coordination.

claims.claim: Sniffing synchronizes with brain oscillations in olfactory regions, hippocampus, amygdala, and neocortex.
claims.source: Sniffing also synchronizes with brain oscillations not only in olfactory regions, but also in hippocampus, amygdala, and neocortex (Karalis and Sirota, 2018; Kay, 2005; Macrides et al., 1982; Vanderwolf, 1992; Yanovsky et al., 2014; Zelano et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Citation of published work on respiration-related brain oscillations.

claims.claim: Respiratory central pattern generators may coordinate sampling movements to synchronize sensory dynamics across modalities with internal brain rhythms.
claims.source: Respiratory central pattern generators may coordinate sampling movements to synchronize sensory dynamics across modalities with internal brain rhythms (Kleinfeld et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Citation of published theoretical work on respiratory coordination.

claims.claim: Locomotor and facial movements drive activity in numerous brain regions including primary sensory areas.
claims.source: Further, locomotor and facial movement, which are often synchronized to respiration, drive activity in numerous brain regions, including primary sensory areas (McGinley et al., 2015; Musall et al., 2019; Niell and Stryker, 2010; Stringer et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Citation of published work on movement-related brain activity.

claims.claim: Sensory systems must disambiguate self-induced stimulus dynamics from changes in the environment.
claims.source: In the real world, sensory receptors operate in closed loop with movement (Ahissar and Assa, 2016; Gibson, 1966). Consequently, sensory systems must disambiguate self-induced stimulus dynamics from changes in the environment.
claims.evidence: Citation of theoretical work on active sensing and sensorimotor integration.

claims.claim: Active sampling movements can provide access to sensory information not otherwise available to a stationary observer.
claims.source: Further, active sampling movements can provide access to sensory information that is not otherwise available to a stationary observer (Gibson, 1962; Schroeder et al., 2010; Yarbus, 1967).
claims.evidence: Citation of theoretical work on active sensing.

claims.claim: Widespread movement-related signals may allow the brain to compensate for and capitalize on self-induced stimulus dynamics.
claims.source: Widespread movement-related signals may allow the brain to compensate for and capitalize on self-induced stimulus dynamics (Poulet and Hedwig, 2006; Sommer and Wurtz, 2008; Sperry, 1950; von Holst and Mittelstaedt, 1950; Webb, 2004).
claims.evidence: Citation of theoretical and empirical work on corollary discharge and sensorimotor integration.

claims.claim: Two-state search strategies are common across phylogeny.
claims.source: Two-state search strategies are common across phylogeny (Bargmann, 2006; Berg, 2000; Kennedy and Marsh, 1974; Lockery, 2011; van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014; Vickers and Baker, 1994).
claims.evidence: Citation of published work on search strategies across multiple species.

claims.claim: State switches in smaller organisms have provided a useful behavioral readout for understanding neural mechanisms of odor-guided behavior.
claims.source: In smaller organisms, state switches have provided a useful behavioral readout for understanding the neural mechanisms of odor-guided behavior (Bi and Sourjik, 2018; Larsch et al., 2015; Baker et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Citation of published work on neural mechanisms of chemotaxis.

claims.claim: Where switches between investigation and approach occur in allocentric space can reveal the location of informative features in an olfactory scene.
claims.source: Here, we have shown that where switches between investigation and approach occur in allocentric space can reveal the location of informative features in an olfactory scene.
claims.evidence: Spatial analysis of state transitions shows they occur preferentially in regions of high gradient discriminability.

claims.claim: Transition points between investigation and approach serve as a principled template for comparing neural activity.
claims.source: The transition points between 'investigation' and 'approach' serve as a principled template against which to compare neural activity.
claims.evidence: The identification of behaviorally relevant transition points provides temporal alignment for neural recordings.

results.result: Mice use concentration gradient cues to navigate turbulent odor plumes in the olfactory search task. Performance decreases with decreasing concentration ratio (ΔC) while remaining constant when absolute concentration varies but gradient is held constant, demonstrating gradient-based rather than absolute concentration-based navigation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C15, C17, and C77 are well-supported by behavioral experiments showing performance varies with concentration gradients (Figure 2D) and equal performance at different absolute concentrations when gradient is constant (90:30 vs 30:10 conditions, Figure 2E). The experimental design effectively dissociates gradient from absolute concentration cues, and statistical tests confirm significant effects.

results.result: Stereo olfaction is not necessary for task performance; mice rely on temporal comparisons across sniffs (serial-sniff strategy) rather than simultaneous bilateral comparisons. Naris occlusion does not significantly impact performance or path tortuosity.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C18, C19, C20, and C82 are supported by naris occlusion experiments (Figure 2F) showing no significant performance deficits (p>0.05). The task design with distant decision line combined with lack of stereo requirement provides converging evidence for serial-sniff comparisons. Statistical tests appropriately control for surgical effects with sham conditions.

results.result: During olfactory search, mice synchronize three-dimensional head movements with sniffing at tens of milliseconds precision. Nose speed peaks at inhalation onset, yaw velocity reaches peak centrifugal velocity at inhalation, and Z-velocity shows coordinated vertical movements with the sniff cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C23-C26, and C64 are well-supported by sniff-aligned kinematic analysis (Figure 5) showing precise temporal coordination between movement parameters and respiration. Permutation testing (p<0.001) confirms synchrony exceeds chance expectations. Cross-correlation and spectral coherence analyses provide additional quantitative support.

results.result: Sniff-synchronized nose movement is a strategic behavioral state selectively deployed during task performance rather than a reflexive accompaniment to fast breathing. Synchrony is present during trials and largely absent during inter-trial intervals, even when controlling for movement speed.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C27-C29 are supported by differential kinematic synchrony between trial and ITI periods (Figure 5), with controls for nose speed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). The presence of synchrony during premature initiation attempts and its reduction post-decision provide additional evidence for strategic deployment. However, the inference of 'strategic' vs 'reflexive' relies on behavioral context rather than direct mechanistic evidence.

results.result: Movement motifs cluster into two behavioral states—investigation and approach—based on transition probabilities. Investigation motifs occur early in trials with slower movement and faster sniffing, while approach motifs occur later. Frequent switches between states suggest continuous evidence integration.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C36-C40 are supported by hierarchical clustering of the transition probability matrix (Figure 7A) revealing two distinct blocks, temporal analysis showing state segregation (Figure 7B-D), and kinematic differences between states (Figure 7E-F). The inference of 'continuous evidence integration' from frequent state switches is reasonable but indirect.

results.result: Investigation motifs lock precisely to the sniff cycle with tens of milliseconds precision, with individual motifs preferentially occurring at specific phases of the sniff cycle. All investigation motifs show significant modulation in both time and phase coordinates.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C45, C46, and C67 are well-supported by motif onset analysis relative to sniff phase (Figure 8) showing significant temporal locking (permutation test, p<0.001). Modulation index analysis demonstrates significant synchrony for all investigation motifs in both time and phase coordinates. The precision is quantitatively demonstrated at the tens of milliseconds scale.

results.result: Correct trials feature increased investigation at and across the midline where odor gradients are steepest, consistent with a serial-sniff gradient sensing strategy. Mice perform best when investigating the location of the steepest slope of the odor gradient rather than directly downwind of odor sources.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C9, C55, C56, C61, C70, C72, and C78 are supported by spatial occupancy analysis (Figure 10) showing significantly increased investigation on the unchosen side of the midline in correct trials (permutation test, p<0.001). The pattern contradicts predictions of absolute concentration strategies and supports serial-sniff comparisons. The analogy to bat echolocation (C71, C73) provides conceptual support but is not direct evidence.

results.result: Investigation is not inherently advantageous irrespective of location. Increased investigation in the transition zone (5-10 cm from initiation) is associated with correct trials, while increased investigation near the decision line or directly downwind of odor sources is associated with incorrect trials, suggesting mice do not capitalize on absolute concentration information.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54, C57, C58, C68, and C69 are supported by spatial analysis of investigation-approach index differences between correct and incorrect trials (Figure 10C, G-I) with permutation testing (p<0.001). The location-dependent association of investigation with performance provides strong evidence against absolute concentration strategies. However, the claim that mice 'cannot capitalize' on absolute concentration (C54) is an inference from negative results.

results.result: The AR-HMM model identifies discrete, recurring movement motifs that capture common features across mice while allowing individual mice to be identified by their motif sequencing patterns. A classifier decoded mouse identity above chance for 8 out of 9 mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C32, and C66 are supported by successful AR-HMM modeling (Figure 6) and linear decoder analysis showing above-chance mouse identification (p<0.01, Figure 6D). The model successfully parsed continuous movement into discrete motifs with interpretable spatiotemporal structure. Cross-validation on held-out trials demonstrates generalization.

results.result: Movement sequences are not statistically distinguishable across different concentration ratios (100:0, 80:20, 60:40), but odor omission trials (0:0) produce distinguishable motif patterns. This suggests mice do not modify their sampling behavior in a gradient-dependent manner in the measured movement parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C35 are supported by linear decoder analysis failing to distinguish concentration ratios but successfully identifying odor omission trials (Figure 6E). However, the conclusion that mice 'do not modify sampling behavior' (C35) is limited to the specific movement parameters measured and may not generalize to other aspects of behavior not captured by the model.

results.result: Mice rapidly learn the olfactory search task, with 24/25 mice performing above chance in the first 100:0 session and 19/26 exceeding 80% performance within four sessions. The behavior generalizes to novel odorants (vanillin) and does not rely on the trigeminal system.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13 are supported by training data (Figure 2B) with appropriate statistical tests (binomial test, p<0.05) and generalization experiments showing equivalent performance with vanillin vs pinene (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=0.827, n=3). The inference about trigeminal independence (C13) is reasonable given vanillin's lack of trigeminal activation, though the small sample size (n=3) limits confidence.

results.result: On odor omission probe trials (0:0), mice perform at chance level with longer trial durations and more tortuous trajectories than odorized trials, confirming behavior is odor-guided.
results.evaluation: Claim C14 is well-supported by statistical testing showing chance-level performance (binomial test, p=0.9989) and significant increases in trial duration and tortuosity (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05, Figure 2C, n=19). This provides strong evidence that performance depends on odor cues.

results.result: Inhalation and sniff durations are shorter during trials than during inter-trial intervals and are strikingly shorter than those observed in head-fixed rodents, indicating qualitatively faster sniffing during freely moving olfactory search.
results.evaluation: Claims C21 and C22 are supported by statistical comparison of sniff parameters between trial and ITI periods (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p<<0.01, Figure 3B-C) and qualitative comparison with published head-fixed data. However, the comparison with head-fixed studies is qualitative rather than quantitative, and differences could reflect task demands rather than movement constraints.

results.result: Investigation and approach states differ in movement speed, sniff rate, and sniff-synchronized kinematic rhythms. During investigation, mice move more slowly, sniff more rapidly, and show greater synchrony of nose speed and yaw velocity with sniffing compared to approach.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 are supported by quantitative comparison between states (Figure 7E-F) with statistical testing (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p<0.01). Permutation testing (p<0.001) confirms kinematic differences exceed expectations from temporal structure alone. The characterization of state-specific kinematic profiles is well-documented.

results.result: Mice primarily investigate near the initiation port and approach close to the decision line, with most state transitions occurring in a transition zone 5-10 cm from the initiation port. The overlap region between investigation and approach is displaced toward the chosen side, indicating mice primarily switch states while located on the side they ultimately choose.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are supported by spatial occupancy analysis (Figure 9) showing distinct spatial distributions of investigation and approach states. The identification of a transition zone is based on inflection points in the investigation-approach index. The displacement toward the chosen side is consistent across individual mice (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).

results.result: Both stay and switch trials show significantly increased investigation at and on the unchosen side of the midline for correct trials, demonstrating that the advantage of sampling across the midline is not an artifact of asymmetry between trial types.
results.evaluation: Claims C59 and C60 are supported by separate analysis of stay and switch trials (Figure 10—figure supplement 1) showing consistent patterns. This control analysis effectively rules out a potential confound in the interpretation of midline sampling advantage, strengthening the serial-sniff hypothesis.

results.result: Mice can navigate noisy gradients formed by turbulent odor plumes, and this gradient-guided search is robust to perturbations including novel odorant introduction and naris occlusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C62 and C63 are supported by successful task performance across multiple experimental manipulations (Figures 2C-F). The characterization of the odor environment as turbulent is supported by PID measurements (Figure 1D, Video 1). This represents a summary conclusion integrating multiple experimental results.

results.result: Movement trajectories are not stereotyped but vary considerably across trials, showing high trial-to-trial variability in nose trajectories.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 is supported by visualization of nose trajectories (Figure 3D) showing qualitatively diverse paths across trials. This observation motivated the use of unsupervised machine learning methods to identify recurring features within variable trajectories.

results.result: Sampling off axis can be an optimal strategy for localization across diverse sensory systems and species, as evidenced by parallels between mouse olfactory search and Egyptian fruit bat echolocation strategies.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 proposes a general principle based on analogy between mouse olfactory search (current data) and bat echolocation (C71, cited work). While the parallel is conceptually interesting and both systems show off-axis sampling at maximum gradient/slope, the evidence is insufficient to establish this as a general principle across 'diverse sensory systems and species' without additional examples and mechanistic understanding.

results.result: Previous studies show that stereo cues may be informative near odor sources where gradients are steep but play less of a role at greater distances where gradients are shallower, with stereo manipulations having small but significant effects in trail following but distance-dependent effects in mole olfactory search.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 accurately summarize findings from cited prior work (Jones and Urban, 2018; Khan et al., 2012; Catania, 2013) on stereo olfaction in different behavioral contexts. These claims represent appropriate contextualization of the current findings within existing literature rather than new results from this study.

results.result: Neurons sensitive to sniff-to-sniff odor concentration changes have been observed in the olfactory bulb of head-fixed mice, providing a potential physiological mechanism for serial-sniff gradient sensing.
results.evaluation: Claim C83 accurately cites published physiological work (Parabucki et al., 2019) demonstrating concentration change-sensitive neurons. This represents appropriate integration of prior physiological findings with current behavioral results to propose a mechanistic hypothesis, though direct evidence linking these neurons to the observed behavior is not provided.

results.result: The external stimulus and sniff statistics in freely moving olfactory search differ dramatically from head-fixed conditions, with qualitatively faster sniffing in freely moving mice. Understanding from head-fixed studies will be incomplete without investigating the fast sniffing regime.
results.evaluation: Claims C84, C85, and C89 are supported by comparison of measured sniff durations with published head-fixed data (Bolding and Franks, 2017; Shusterman et al., 2011; Wesson et al., 2009). The argument for studying freely moving conditions is logical, though the claim that head-fixed understanding will be 'incomplete' (C89) is a value judgment about research priorities rather than an empirical finding.
